title: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on what makes a firm 'AI-first'
author: Jen Berrent

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Berrent shifts the focus from contract intelligence as a business-coordination layer to the provider’s delivery model: first decide whether the offering is software, people, or both, then build technology around that choice. Her model integrates back-end efficiency, client interaction and legal outputs, combining direct-to-client software with legal expertise embedded at different stages. Abramowitz separately frames incumbent retrofitting as a potential obstacle to becoming AI-first.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jen Berrent presents AI-first legal services as a deliberately redesigned, software-led delivery model that embeds lawyer expertise, reduces transaction processing and outside-counsel involvement, and competes for work currently handled by large firms.
pts.d: Berrent makes the following claims and predictions. (1) An AI-first firm builds its operations, client experience and business model around AI from inception, rather than merely adding AI to existing legal workflows. Direct-to-client software should incorporate legal expertise throughout delivery. (2) Covenant uses multiple models to review agreements, matches their answers, applies AI-based quality assurance and then lawyer verification. She claims this process reaches 100% accuracy and predicts that the cost and time required to reach that level will decrease as models improve. This is her claim about the combined workflow, not a claim that an unaided model is perfectly accurate. (3) AI can move beyond document summaries to advice-like outputs: lawyers program relationships between contractual points and the issues to flag, while clients' historical deal positions can inform advice automatically. Clients should be able to access and query their knowledge rather than depend on a law firm as its gatekeeper. (4) Embedding more advice into verified results lets clients complete more transactions themselves, reducing outside lawyers' work per transaction. Berrent reports an increase in Covenant's self-service transaction share from 55% in the first quarter to 90% at the beginning of October, while expecting it to settle around 80%. Self-service here means less additional Covenant assistance, not absence of the firm's underlying lawyer verification. (5) Most traditional law-firm operating software is, in her view, unnecessary baggage for Covenant's model. Transaction-based billing and platform-user onboarding require different infrastructure; Covenant built its own client matter management system. She expects document comparison to remain useful but anticipates something different from current track-changes exchanges. (6) She predicts fewer jobs processing legal paperwork, including routine redlining, and greater importance for substantive judgment, understanding differences in language, anticipating transactions, configuring AI's analysis and using deal data. She also proposes connecting legal terms to deal performance rather than relying on anecdotal assertions of what is market. (7) She predicts that low-end commercial contracting will become almost entirely software-based without needing lawyers, while AI-first firms can take core transactional work currently flowing to Big Law because there is no satisfactory middle-market alternative. She explicitly does not expect Covenant to compete for the most bespoke public M&A, highly regulated transactions or largest complex fund formations. (8) Covenant's growth thesis is vertical-by-vertical coverage of private-market transactions, starting with fund investors and expanding to venture investors. Taking one side of transactions is intended to reduce conflicts and enable a SaaS-like claim on all of a client's relevant deals. (9) AI-driven speed and savings do not eliminate clients' need for trust and an accountable legal backstop. (10) Berrent says technology must reflect whether a business sells software, people-delivered work or a combination. She claims providers starting with NDAs or commercial contracts struggle to move into more complex work, motivating Covenant's harder but narrower starting product.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of Berrent's account of Covenant's operations, a self-reported service-usage trend, concrete pricing and delivery terms, and her professional experience; broader predictions are supported by reasoning and analogies rather than independent studies.
pts.d: For the delivery-model claims, Berrent describes a specific workflow: multiple models answer approximately 120 questions about an agreement; answers are compared, checked by an AI judge and verified by a lawyer; groups of five to eight related points are then interpreted using lawyer-programmed guidance. She provides no benchmark results, sample size, error definition or independent validation for the claimed 100% accuracy. Her principal quantitative support for reduced additional lawyer involvement is Covenant's reported shift from 45% full-service add-ons and 55% self-service in the first quarter to 90% self-service transactions at the beginning of October. Her initial wording mixes clients and deals, before describing the later figure explicitly as transactions. No transaction counts, client-composition data or controlled attribution are supplied. She attributes the shift to tools containing more legal commentary and verified information. The product example is a $900 LPA review delivered in two days, with add-ons and a small, declining amount of hourly work. This illustrates Covenant's reported operating model, not a measured comparison with incumbent prices or lawyer hours. For infrastructure redesign, she cites the practical difficulty of billing even a dozen clients using existing approaches and describes the in-house client matter management platform, while acknowledging substantial use of off-the-shelf backend services. For the continued role of trust, she reports that every client has met her or her partner Richard. For judgment, negotiation and deal-data claims, she draws on her experience as a law-firm partner and WeWork legal executive, including manually charting prior financing terms, preferred future positions and possible trade-offs. Analogies include Amazon building around warehouses rather than stores, E Trade changing client engagement once trust is established, and Excel reducing manual accounting work. Predictions about fewer processing jobs, software-only low-end contracting, displacement of Big Law's core work, greater use of outcome data and providers' difficulty moving upstream are not accompanied by systematic labor-market data, comparative studies or named supporting cases.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Berrent distinguishes Covenant's current practices from undated predictions about improving AI, employment and market structure; the self-service comparison is within the interview year, presented as 2025 in the document.
pts.d: The multi-model workflow, lawyer verification, proprietary management platform, fixed-fee product and personal client relationships are described as existing at the interview date. The self-service comparison runs from the first quarter of that year to the beginning of October; given the document's 2025 attribution, this implies 2025, although Berrent does not independently state the year in the passage. Her expectation that self-service will level off at 80% is a forecast, distinct from the reported October observation of 90%. Falling verification cost and turnaround time are conditional on models improving within Covenant's deliberately designed workflow; she does not provide a deadline or measured reduction. Client autonomy depends on trusted, verified answers and lawyer-programmed commentary. She particularly emphasizes in-house lawyers' ability to finish transactions, while saying nonlawyers can decide issues framed clearly as business choices. Current coverage is investments into funds on the LP side, not GP fund formation; Covenant does not provide regulatory or tax work, which may require traditional firms. Negotiation can require separate assistance, and some residual work is billed hourly. Expansion into venture investing on the investor side is described as the next market, with no date. Predictions of fewer processing jobs, almost entirely software-based low-end commercial contracting, changed document-markup tools and competitive redistribution of transactional work have no explicit horizon. Continued personal relationship-building is expressly a current condition, not a claim that software can never acquire clients directly. Berrent preserves a role for entirely bespoke, elite transactions and significant legal judgment. She expects Covenant probably to raise more funding for execution speed, new verticals and product development, but says large fundraising is not intrinsically required for the business and disclaims a race for massive funding.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes primarily concern institutional private-market clients, their in-house teams, transactional lawyers and large firms' core deal practices, rather than individual access to justice.
pts.d: Covenant's current target is allocators investing into private funds: endowments, foundations, family offices, sovereign wealth funds and other owners of capital, typically with approximately $1 billion in assets under management up to the largest sovereign funds. These clients receive fixed-price reviews, access to structured contractual information and commentary, and the ability to complete more deals without further outside-counsel assistance. In-house lawyers gain access to expertise previously obtainable through hourly conversations; business decision-makers may resolve clearly explained commercial risks themselves. Outside lawyers doing repeatable document processing face less work per transaction and, in Berrent's forecast, fewer processing jobs. Lawyers exercising substantive judgment, anticipating negotiation priorities, designing analytical guidance and interpreting data become more important; she does not quantify total profession-wide employment effects. Large firms face potential competition for core transactional work between commercial contracts and public M&A, including the kinds of $20 million M&A and Series A transactions she identifies as poorly matched to Big Law's model. Elite bespoke deal practices remain differentiated in her account. Covenant itself aims for a lean legal and administrative organization, with less manual billing effort and growth through specialized transaction verticals. Traditional legal software providers face a claimed mismatch between incumbent-oriented systems and AI-first operating requirements, although Covenant still purchases ordinary backend services. Software and legal-service businesses face strategic choices about product scope, delivery responsibility and how starting at the low-complexity end may constrain perceived capability. The source does not make a concrete claim about reducing the civil justice gap or improving legal access for underserved individuals.
